“Assessing the effects of different lunar soil mixtures and concentrations on 
the germination and growth of Spinacia oleracea” 
 
 
 
Team: Sunburst Big Brains 
Sunburst MT, 59482 
Instructor: Amanda Nix

Purpose 
The purpose of this experiment is to determine the most effective soil additive to combine with 
lunar soil with the end goal of growing plants in a lunar colony with most efficiency. 
 
Question 
What soil additive (Organic Compost, Liquid Fertilizer, or Potting Soil) will be most effective 
for adding to lunar simulation soil to encourage the growth of spinach seeds? 
 
Hypothesis 
Our team hypothesized that the soil composition with the organic compost would have the most 
noticeable effect on the growth of spinach, as measured by variables including germination rate, 
seedling height over the growth period, number of leaves, average leaf surface area, and dry 
mass weight. 
 
Experimental Design 
1. Set up the growth chamber, creating a 12 hours on, 12 hours off light cycle to simulate a 
day-night cycle. 
2. Document light intensity in lumens using a LabQuest device 
3. Equip personal protective equipment (M95 masks) to prevent dust related injuries 
4. Cover the bottom of the pots (approximately 1 inch deep) with pea gravel for aeration 
and drainage. 
5. Create soil mixtures using (A) Potting Soil with lunar regolith, (B) Potting Soil, liquid 
fertilizer, and lunar regolith, and ( C) Compost with lunar regolith 
6. Note: Mix liquid fertilizer with spring water according to instructions on fertilizer 
7. Mix each type of additive (A-C) with the moon regolith in varying concentrations, that of 
10% additive, 20%, 30%, 40%, and 50%, such that each type of soil mixture has five 
different concentrations 
8. Check the pH of each soil variety, in each concentration. 
9. Plant spinach seeds, five seeds in each type and concentration of soil mixture 
10. Water each set of soil mixtures with 10 mL of spring water 3 times a week. 
11. Note: Halfway through the growth period, we increased water consumption to 20 mL 
spring water, five times per week, due to lack of germination. 
12. Document germination rates for each type of soil mixture and concentration 
13. After seeds have germinated, thin each soil concentration to just one growing plant to 
make the most efficient use of materials. 
14. Note: Did not accomplish step 15, as honestly, we kind of forgot about it 
15. Check the pH of each soil once a week, on Mondays (before watering) 
16. Document seedling height, number of leaves, and average leaf surface area each week. 
17. At the end of the growth period, measure the dry mass weight of each plant. 
18. Analyze all data

Conclusion 
At the conclusion of this experiment, results showed that no plants germinated in the 
lunar soil control and plants successfully germinated in each of the other soil mixtures, except for 
Potting Soil 20% for unknown reasons. While the soil mixtures all seemed to germinate at 
similar rates, the leaf lengths were drastically different. The most notable growth occurred in the 
soil mixtures of natural compost. In addition, as the lunar soil percentage increased in the potting 
soil and the fertilizer mixtures, germination and survivability of plants diminished. In the natural 
compost, however, more seeds germinated and survived longer. In addition, the length of leaves 
and height of plants were statistically higher across the concentrations of the compost soil 
additive as compared to the fertilizer, potting soil, and lunar control. 
 
Discussion 
 
The analysis of the data gathered has allowed us to draw several conclusions. First of all, 
we can accept our original hypothesis that the organic compost would have the most noticeable 
effect on the growth of spinach, as measured by certain variables. The compost germination rates 
were not the fastest rates, as the fertilizer boosts germination, but the compost did yield the most 
complete germination, with the majority of each percentage having 4-5 germinated plants. 
 
This support of the hypothesis assists with the idea of efficiency of growing plants in a 
lunar colony. Because the organic compost is made of natural substances, any excess food or 
other organic material can be reused to grow more plants. In addition, less initial compost 
(compared to potting soil) would be needed to begin a farm, as more compost can be made on 
site at the colony. 
 
Some of the issues we ran into during the growth period included water and survivability 
of plants. During the initial first half of the growth period. Approximately four total plants grew, 
and only in the controls of potting soil and compost. We analyzed the appearance of the soils and 
noticed a drainage issue. It seemed that the soil did not hold water well and the soil always 
looked very parched. We replanted the spinach seeds and increased the water schedule to 20mL 
per day, five days per week. We kept all other variables the same and within the next several 
days, strong new growth occurred in nearly every concentration of every soil mixture. 
 
One of the issues with documentation is that we only documented the germination of the 
plants and not the deaths of the plants. Once they germinated, we marked them down. Because of 
this, the germination numbers do not exactly match up with the final measurements. 
 
Despite these issues, it seems that the project was a successful way to analyze the basic 
differences between soil additives to lunar soil. With that being said, it seems that the most 
effective method for improving lunar soil for growing plants in a lunar environment is an organic 
compost.
